item.content:encoded:
Regrettably not; I have no idea how they work beyond what's described in the article. See this reply-chain (contained in this very thread!) for more details regarding the inverted bell-curve approach, though.

TL;DR: Roll (at least) three dice, then flip a coin. Heads, take the highest roll; tails, take the lowest. This results in a distribution of probability where 'extreme' results — high and low rolls — become more likely than 'middle' results. Basically, in simple RPG terms… critical hits and critical misses become more likely; normal hits and normal misses become more rare.

For more information on this, you can take a look at this thread (on rpg.stackexchange); the first response goes into more detail, and explains some alternative methods to achieve a similar result.

item.title: My first thought was "Ohey it's Kieron Gillen's DiE but actually good."
item.content:encoded: The title is actually an awful comparison, as the description of the game and its paranormal(?) side are vastly different from anything in the comic. However it still holds that I enjoyed this piece significantly more, as it actually delivered on the horror aspect that DiE never did. It's intriguing and more than a little unsettling to see what might well be an anafabula-in-progress as an alternative perspective to the usual second hand recordings of a work that's long since fulfilled the complete criteria and been annihilated (Parawatch having given us two of those already).

item.content:encoded:
I like this premise a lot, and the overall description of the game seems pretty interesting. However, I have to agree with what others stated. It's typical for creepypastas like this one to have a kinda logical explanation for what happened, thus luring us into a false sense of security. But usually, we are given some hints as to why those explanations don't work well enough. Something that doesn't add up. However in this case, the explanation works so well that we don't have a reason to believe that there's something more to this game, and that there's paranormal stuff going on with the minotaur.

Due to this, the creepypasta didn't have much impact on me, and I see this as a problem because creepypastas are meant to evoke some uneasy emotions. Novote.

Inverted bell-curves can be tricky to grasp unless you've got some basic background in probabilities. Even most nerds might miss what's going on when I tell them to "roll two dice, then flip a coin — heads, take the low roll; tails, take the high roll".

As for the rest — a lot of what's going on here (and how this works) isn't elaborated on in the article. That's intentional; I didn't want the article to describe an anomaly so much as hint at one.

Your spoiler makes little sense. There are players that are analyzing the game up until 2012, which means the games are played and there are people witnessing the result of the games, otherwise the game would've died down long ago. The nerds that are playing the games should also discovered the probability proportion between Escape Hex and Minotaur early in the game. I think it's also implied that the community simply gradually stopped playing new games after the probability thing is discovered.

Also…the final thread really shouldn't matter much for the community, beyond fascination to the original copy, that can't really be confirmed since there's also the chance that the kid's copy is the modified one that removed the Minotaur. It's 2012, everyone could get access to old papers and a printer. Say that the original copy don't have Minotaur and it's added by some homebrew rules. So what? It exist now. Same with the aspect of this Wiki: Parawatch is now a thing, O5 is a thing, GOC etc is a thing, that didn't exist in 173.

A lot of this is operating on elision. I might tweak a few things to make it more clear what's going on, but to clarify — the people playing this game weren't playing it for fun. To wit:

Spoiler
– hide block

Nevertheless, it retained a small and active audience who sought to outwit the cruel and relentless Minotaur.

Once you died (either from a trap, starvation, or the Minotaur), the hex you perished in was marked.

item.content:encoded: I enjoyed this enough to upvote on atmosphere and mechanics, but the creepiness of it (which I assume was the main thrust?) felt extremely subdued, largely because the weird thing is entirely explainable. It's noted early in the article that there was lots of fanbrewing to fill gaps in the product, so something weird showing up that wasn't in the base game feels expected. The fact that everything operates according to arcane probability tables also seems to explain how the minotaur could always arrive to deflect players approaching victory. I'm not sure if you want the punch to be stronger or not, but it seems like it definitely could be.
